criteria.name: Q1 Quality attributes
criteria.reasoning: Performance and availability are well justified from the lunch-hour scenario. Both scenarios have six parts, but the availability response measure ('stay up most of the time') is not measurable, so this is Proficient rather than Excellent.

evidence.quote: Response measure: the system should stay up most of the time.

criteria.name: Q2 Architectural style
criteria.reasoning: Clear modular-monolith recommendation with scenario-specific trade-offs (five-developer team, single-VM and deployment-downtime problems). The downside is explicitly acknowledged.

evidence.quote: With five developers, running eight or ten services would mean more time spent on infrastructure than on features.
The trade-off I accept is that modules cannot be scaled independently

criteria.name: Q3 Availability calculation
criteria.reasoning: Part (a) is correct (99.30%). Part (b) is wrong: 0.00699 × 720 ≈ 5.0 h, not 3.5 h. Part (c) is wrong: it reports payment availability as end-to-end order availability, ignoring the 99.30% chain, giving about 99.30% and roughly 5.1 h/month. Two parts are incorrect.

evidence.quote: So the new availability of placing an order is 99.9975%

criteria.name: Q4 Resilience pattern
criteria.reasoning: Circuit breaker is an appropriate pattern with a tuning consideration. However the state mechanism is wrong: Closed passes calls through, Open fails fast, and the text reverses them. Half-Open success is also described as reopening the breaker. The explanation is incorrect.

evidence.quote: In the Open state calls pass through normally.
the breaker moves to Closed and calls fail immediately

criteria.name: Q5 Consistency and availability
criteria.reasoning: Choices are reasoned, and a concrete technique is named for menu browsing. The CAP explanation is imprecise: partition tolerance cannot be given up in a distributed system. No concrete technique is named for the payment/order case.

evidence.quote: so for payments we choose consistency and availability and give up partition tolerance.

criteria.name: Q6 Architecture decision record
criteria.reasoning: Context, Decision and Consequences are all present and scenario-specific. Consequences are entirely positive; no negative consequence (e.g., added complexity, eventual delivery, queue failure handling) is given.

evidence.quote: Consequences: Placing an order no longer waits for the outlet, so the response time improves.

criteria.name: Communication and format
criteria.reasoning: Word limits and headings are met and the writing is clear. Citation [2] is used but absent from the reference list, which is a citation problem.

evidence.quote: The Circuit Breaker pattern [2] would have contained the failure.
[1] L. Bass, P. Clements, and R. Kazman

technical_issues.issue: Downtime 0.00699 × 720 is about 5.0 h, not 3.5 h.
End-to-end availability ignores the 99.30% order chain and is reported as 99.9975%; correct value is about 99.30% with roughly 5.1 h/month downtime.
Circuit breaker states are wrong: Closed passes calls, Open fails fast, Half-Open success should close the breaker.
Claiming to give up partition tolerance is incorrect; in distributed systems partitions must be tolerated, so the choice is between C and A during a partition.
Availability response measure is not measurable.
No explicit assumptions stated, as required by R7.

overall: Good structure and a sound architecture recommendation, but Question 3 has two incorrect parts, the circuit breaker mechanism and CAP explanation contain errors, and the ADR lacks negative consequences. Availability measure is not measurable, reference [2] is missing, and no assumptions are stated.

feedback.summary: Strong, well-structured answers overall, and your Question 2 modular-monolith recommendation is the standout piece — clearly argued with scenario-specific trade-offs. The work needed now is precision: two parts of Question 3 are arithmetically wrong, the circuit breaker states are reversed in Question 4, the CAP explanation in Question 5 misstates what can be sacrificed, and your ADR needs a negative consequence. Fixing these is mostly mechanical rather than conceptual.
next_steps: Redo Question 3(b) and (c) with the arithmetic written out: 0.00699 × 720 ≈ 5.0 h, and for (c) multiply the whole order chain (including the 99.30% outlet availability) rather than reporting payment availability alone, giving ≈99.30% and about 5.1 h/month downtime.
Rewrite the Question 4 mechanism so the states are correct: Closed lets calls through, Open fails fast, and a successful Half-Open trial closes the breaker. Keep your tuning consideration as-is.

Revisit Question 5 so partition tolerance is treated as unavoidable in a distributed system — the choice is between C and A during a partition — and name a concrete technique for the payment/order case as well as for menu browsing.

For Question 6, add at least one negative consequence (for example added queue complexity or handling broker failure), and replace the Question 1 availability response measure with something measurable such as a percentage uptime target.
Replace the missing reference [2] with a full IEEE-style entry, state your assumptions explicitly, and re-check every response measure is stated in numbers.
Keep your Question 2 reasoning as the model for the rest — that paragraph is exactly the level of specificity the rubric rewards.

criteria.C1: Your performance and availability choices are well justified from the lunch-hour peak, and both scenarios are complete in structure. The gap to Excellent is measurability: 'stay up most of the time' cannot be tested. Restate it as a numeric uptime target over a defined period and this becomes Excellent.
criteria.C2: Excellent work. The modular-monolith recommendation is specific to the five-developer team and the single-VM, deployment-downtime problems, and you explicitly accept that modules cannot be scaled independently. This is exactly the trade-off reasoning the rubric asks for.
criteria.C3: Part (a) is correct at 99.30%, but (b) misstates 0.00699 × 720 as 3.5 h when it is about 5.0 h, and (c) reports payment availability as end-to-end order availability. For (c), the full order chain including the 99.30% outlet gives about 99.30% and roughly 5.1 h/month. Show your working line by line.
criteria.C4: Circuit breaker is the right pattern and your tuning consideration is sound, but the state machine is described backwards: Closed passes calls, Open fails fast, and Half-Open success closes the breaker. Correct the mechanism and this answer reaches the top level.
criteria.C5: Your choices are reasoned and the Redis 60-second TTL is a concrete, appropriate technique for menu browsing. Two fixable gaps: partition tolerance cannot be given up in a distributed system, so frame the choice as C versus A during a partition; and name a concrete technique for the payment/order case too.
criteria.C6: Context, Decision and Consequences are all present and tied to the CampusEats scenario. The consequences read entirely positively, though. Add at least one negative consequence — added queue complexity, or what happens if the broker fails — and it becomes Excellent.
criteria.C7: Word limits and headings are respected and the writing is clear throughout. The one problem is citation [2] in Question 4 being absent from your reference list. Add the full IEEE-style entry and this criterion is fully met.
